newsitem.title: USA: Dollar finishes mixed in U.S. trading.
newsitem.headline: Dollar finishes mixed in U.S. trading.

text.p: The dollar ended marginally higher after news of a fire at a nuclear fuel processing plant in Japan weighed on the yen, but the U.S. currency failed to hold on to very early gains versus the mark, experts said.
Ten workers at Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp's Tokaimura plant located north of Tokyo were exposed to radiation when a small fire broke out on Tuesday morning.

The news contributed to the dollar's "bid tone" but it was not the entire reason why the dollar went higher, said Thomas Arnold, a vice president and chief dealer of foreign exchange at Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank in New York.
Some traders also noted talk of a large purchase of dollars for yen by a bank during New York trading.

Initially, the dollar fell versus the yen in Asia after a government report showed private-sector machinery orders in Japan, excluding orders for machinery at electric power firms and for ships, jumped a robust 11.8 percent in January from the previous month.
In New York, the dollar closed at 121.80/90 yen, slightly higher than 121.74/79 yen at the open. Against the German currency, the dollar fell to 1.7045/55 from 1.7063/68.
The dollar drifted lower in New York dealings even though dwindling concern about a possible postponement to European monetary union pressured the mark very early in the session.
Comments from Bundesbank council members late on Monday insisted the single European currency, the Euro, should begin as planned on January 1, 1999.

"What caused the mark to weaken was less fear in the market of a delay," said Elliott Dix, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Signet Bank. "There was less fear in the market because of the comments from the Bundesbank officials."

Bundesbank council member Guntram Palm said recent speculation about a possible delay to the debut of the single currency was "totally misplaced" and he expects a majority of European Union countries to meet the entry criteria.

Another council member Ernst Welteke said the Euro could take place as planned in 1999 without weakening the membership criteria. He explained the entry standards allow for small deviations from targets for public deficits.
To qualify for single currency, countries must slash their public deficits to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product and reduce total debt towards 60 percent of GDP.

Still, dollar/mark turned lower as market players awaited a flood of U.S. economic reports including the Federal Reserve's Beige Book due out Wednesday at 1400 EST/1900 GMT and U.S. retail sales for February and the fourth-quarter current account deficit on Thursday.
"People are waiting for the numbers later on this week," said Doug Lee, an assistant vice president at Sakura Bank Ltd in New York. "(There was) really no news...out today."
In other trade, the dollar fell to 1.4715/25 Swiss francs at the close from 1.4745/55 at the open. Sterling rose to $1.6062/72 from $1.6040/50.
The dollar also slid to Canadian $1.3669/74 from C$1.3680/85.
The Australian dollar ended at $0.7930/35, up from $0.7918/23.
